books.title: Curiosity: Textbook of Science for Grade 7

source.method: chapter titles from the book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's section headings

topics.title: The Ever-Evolving World of Science
objectives: Student can explain that science is a process and a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, questions and the unknown
Student can explain why the fields of science in the book (physics, chemistry, biology, earth sciences) are interconnected
Student can name some of the themes the book explores, such as materials, changes, heat, life processes, time, light and the Earth, Moon and Sun
visualIdeas: a paper plane and a butterfly flying across pages linked to the chapter themes
a web joining physics, chemistry, biology and earth science bubbles

topics.title: Happy Exploring!
objectives: Student can explain why asking interesting questions is as important as finding answers in science
Student can make up creative questions that could lead to a given answer, as in the Question the Answer activity
visualIdeas: an answer card such as "Just add some milk" with several different question bubbles leading to it

chapters.title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

topics.title: Litmus as an Indicator
objectives: Student can test everyday samples such as lemon juice, soap solution and sugar solution with blue and red litmus paper
Student can classify substances as acidic (blue litmus turns red), basic (red litmus turns blue) or neutral (no change)
Student can state that litmus is a natural substance obtained from lichens and is used as an acid-base indicator
visualIdeas: a white tile with drops of different samples on blue and red litmus pieces
a three-column sorting chart: acidic, basic, neutral

topics.title: Red Rose as an Indicator
objectives: Student can describe how an indicator is prepared from red rose petals
Student can state that red rose extract gives a red colour in acidic solutions and a green colour in basic solutions
visualIdeas: crushed red rose petals in hot water turning into an extract
two test tubes showing red and green colours

topics.title: Turmeric as an Indicator
objectives: Student can prepare turmeric paper strips and use them to test samples
Student can state that turmeric turns red in basic solutions and stays yellow in acidic and neutral solutions
Student can explain the hidden message at the science fair using turmeric and a soap solution
visualIdeas: a yellow turmeric strip turning red where soap solution touches it
a white sheet revealing a hidden message when sprayed

topics.title: What Happens When Acidic Substances Mix with Basic Substances?
objectives: Student can describe the colour change of an indicator as lime water is added drop by drop to diluted lemon juice
Student can define neutralisation as the reaction between an acid and a base that forms salt and water and gives out heat
visualIdeas: a test tube with litmus solution changing colour as drops of lime water are added
acid + base -> salt + water + heat as a word equation

topics.title: Neutralisation in Daily Life
objectives: Student can explain why moist baking soda relieves the sting of a red ant bite, which injects formic acid
Student can explain how acidic soil is treated with lime and basic soil with organic matter
Student can suggest neutralising acidic factory waste before it is released into a lake
visualIdeas: three situation cards: ant bite, soil treatment, factory waste entering a lake

topics.title: A Torchlight
objectives: Student can identify the lamp, cells and switch of a torchlight
Student can explain that the torch lamp glows in one position of the switch and not in the other
visualIdeas: a torch with its lamp, cells and switch labelled

topics.title: Electric Cell and Battery
objectives: Student can identify the positive terminal (metal cap) and negative terminal (flat metal disc) of an electric cell
Student can explain that a battery is a combination of cells placed with the positive terminal of one next to the negative terminal of the next
visualIdeas: an electric cell with + and - terminals marked
two cells joined in a row inside a torch compartment

topics.title: Electric Lamp
objectives: Student can describe the filament of an incandescent lamp, which gets hot and glows when current passes through it
Student can explain that an LED has a longer positive wire and a shorter negative wire and lets current pass in one direction only
visualIdeas: cut-away of an incandescent bulb showing the filament and its two terminals
an LED with long (+) and short (-) legs

topics.title: An Electrical Circuit
objectives: Student can connect a cell, wires and a lamp so that the lamp glows
Student can explain that a circuit is a complete path from one terminal of the cell, through the lamp, to the other terminal
Student can state that the direction of current is taken from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell
visualIdeas: a cell holder, lamp holder and wires forming a closed loop with arrows showing current

topics.title: Electric Switch
objectives: Student can make a simple switch using drawing pins and a safety pin
Student can explain that a switch completes or breaks a circuit
visualIdeas: a homemade switch shown in OFF and ON positions

topics.title: Circuit Diagrams
objectives: Student can draw the symbols for a cell, battery, lamp, LED, switch (ON and OFF) and wire
Student can draw the circuit diagram of a simple circuit such as a torch
visualIdeas: a table of circuit symbols
a torch circuit redrawn as a circuit diagram

topics.title: Electrical Conductors and Insulators
objectives: Student can use a tester circuit to sort materials into conductors and insulators
Student can explain why wires are made of metal and covered with plastic or rubber
Student can list safety precautions with electricity, such as never touching switches with wet hands
visualIdeas: a tester circuit with a gap where different objects are placed
a sorting chart of conductors and insulators

chapters.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals

topics.title: Malleability
objectives: Student can observe lustre and hardness of materials such as copper, aluminium, iron, coal and sulfur
Student can define malleability as the property of being beaten into thin sheets and identify it as a property of metals
visualIdeas: a hammer flattening an aluminium piece next to a piece of coal that crumbles

topics.title: Ductility and Sonority
objectives: Student can define ductility as the property of being drawn into wires and give examples like copper wires
Student can describe sonority as the ringing sound metals make when struck, compared with wood or coal
visualIdeas: metal wires used in a sitar or veena
a metal spoon and a block of wood dropped side by side with sound waves

topics.title: Conduction of Heat and Electricity
objectives: Student can explain why cooking vessels are made of metals, based on how a metal spoon and a wooden spoon heat up in hot water
Student can use a tester circuit to show that metals are good conductors of electricity and materials like sulfur, coal and wood are poor conductors
visualIdeas: a metal spoon and a wooden spoon standing in hot water
a tester circuit with a bulb glowing for an iron nail

topics.title: Effect of Air and Water on Metals: Iron
objectives: Student can describe the three-bottle experiment showing that iron forms a brown deposit (rust) only when both air and water are present
Student can define corrosion as the damage to metal objects exposed to moist air
visualIdeas: three bottles: nail with silica gel, nail in boiled water under oil, nail partly in water and open to air

topics.title: Effect of Air and Water on Other Metals
objectives: Student can describe how a magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame to form magnesium oxide
Student can show with litmus that the solution of a metal oxide is basic
Student can explain why sodium is stored in kerosene
visualIdeas: a burning magnesium ribbon held with tongs
red litmus turning blue in magnesium oxide solution

topics.title: Substances that Behave Differently from Metals in Air and Water
objectives: Student can describe how burning sulfur forms sulfur dioxide whose solution in water is acidic
Student can state that sulfur does not react with water and that phosphorus is stored in water
Student can list properties of non-metals: usually soft, dull, not malleable or ductile, and poor conductors
visualIdeas: sulfur burning in a deflagrating spoon inside a covered gas jar
blue litmus turning red

topics.title: Are Non-metals Essential in Everyday Life?
objectives: Student can explain why non-metals such as oxygen and carbon are essential for life
Student can list some everyday uses of metals and non-metals
visualIdeas: a chart of everyday uses of metals and non-metals

chapters.title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

topics.title: A Substance May Change in Appearance but Remain the Same!
objectives: Student can explain, using examples like folding paper or melting ice, that a change in shape, size or state need not form a new substance
Student can define a physical change as one in which no new substance is formed
visualIdeas: paper folded into a boat and unfolded back
ice melting and water freezing in a cycle

topics.title: A Substance May Change in Appearance and Not Remain the Same!
objectives: Student can describe how exhaled air turns lime water milky, showing a new substance is formed
Student can define a chemical change as one in which one or more new substances are formed, represented by a chemical equation
visualIdeas: two tumblers, tap water and lime water, with a straw blowing exhaled air into each

topics.title: Rusting and Combustion
objectives: Student can explain why rusting of iron and burning of a magnesium ribbon are chemical changes
Student can state that combustion gives out heat and/or light and define ignition temperature
Student can name the three things needed for fire using the fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and heat
visualIdeas: the fire triangle with fuel, oxygen and heat on its sides
a rusted iron nail beside a burning magnesium ribbon

topics.title: Can Physical and Chemical Changes Occur in the Same Process?
objectives: Student can explain how a burning candle involves both a physical change (melting of wax) and a chemical change (burning of wax)
Student can classify the melting of wax as a physical change and the burning of wax as a chemical change
visualIdeas: a lit candle with melting wax labelled physical and the flame labelled chemical

topics.title: Are Changes Permanent?
objectives: Student can sort everyday changes into those that can be reversed and those that cannot
Student can explain, with examples like melting and cooking, why some changes cannot be reversed
visualIdeas: a two-column table: reversible (melting) and irreversible (cooking)

topics.title: Are All Changes Desirable?
objectives: Student can give examples of desirable changes such as curdling of milk and ripening of fruit
Student can give examples of undesirable changes such as rusting and decay of stored food
visualIdeas: two baskets labelled desirable and undesirable with picture cards

topics.title: Some Slow Natural Changes
objectives: Student can explain weathering as the breaking of rocks into sediments by temperature changes, roots and freezing water, along with chemical changes
Student can explain erosion as the movement of broken rock and soil by wind and flowing water
visualIdeas: a mountain base with heaps of sediments
a river carrying pebbles that become smooth

chapters.title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change

topics.title: Growing With Age: The Teenage Years
objectives: Student can define adolescence as the period of change from childhood to adulthood, generally from about 10 to 19 years
Student can list physical changes during adolescence and explain secondary sexual characteristics
Student can define puberty
visualIdeas: a growth timeline from childhood through adolescence to adulthood

topics.title: Changes that Indicate Reproductive Capability
objectives: Student can explain that internal changes in adolescence include the maturing of parts involved in reproduction
Student can describe menstruation as the discharge of blood generally every 28-30 days, beginning at puberty
visualIdeas: a calendar marking a 28-30 day cycle

topics.title: Emotional and Behavioural Changes in Adolescents
objectives: Student can list emotional changes in adolescence and their possible effects on behaviour
Student can suggest positive ways to handle these changes
visualIdeas: a table of emotional changes, effects and positive responses

topics.title: Meeting Nutritional Needs and Personal Hygiene
objectives: Student can explain why a balanced diet with proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals matters during adolescence
Student can describe personal hygiene practices, including menstrual hygiene
visualIdeas: a balanced plate for an adolescent
a hygiene checklist

topics.title: Physical Activities and a Balanced Social Life
objectives: Student can explain how regular exercise keeps the body and mind fit and boosts mood
Student can describe respectful and responsible behaviour in person and on social media
visualIdeas: children playing sports
a respectful conversation between friends

topics.title: Avoiding Harmful Substances: Learn to Say NO
objectives: Student can explain the harmful effects of tobacco, alcohol and drugs on body and mind
Student can practise ways to say NO to peer pressure
visualIdeas: a speech bubble saying NO to a hand offering a cigarette

topics.title: The 'Why' Question for Adolescence
objectives: Student can explain that changes in adolescence are mainly controlled by hormones, chemicals produced in the body
Student can explain how guidance and awareness help adolescents manage these changes
visualIdeas: a body outline with arrows from glands to the changes they control

topics.title: Conduction of Heat
objectives: Student can explain the pins-on-a-metal-strip activity, where the pin nearest the flame falls first
Student can define conduction as heat transfer from the hotter to the colder part of an object without the particles moving from their positions
Student can classify materials as good conductors (metals) or poor conductors (insulators) of heat such as wood, glass and clay
visualIdeas: a metal strip with wax-stuck pins falling one by one away from a candle

topics.title: Convection
objectives: Student can explain why hot air rises using the paper cups balanced over a candle
Student can describe convection currents in heated water shown by potassium permanganate
Student can state that in liquids and gases heat is transferred mainly by convection, through the movement of particles
visualIdeas: two paper cups on a stick, one rising over a candle
a beaker with a coloured streak rising in the middle and sinking at the sides

topics.title: Land and Sea Breeze
objectives: Student can explain from an experiment that soil heats up and cools down faster than water
Student can explain how the sea breeze blows during the day and the land breeze at night
visualIdeas: day and night coastal diagrams with arrows for sea breeze and land breeze

topics.title: Radiation
objectives: Student can explain that radiation transfers heat without a medium, as from the Sun or a fire
Student can explain why light-coloured clothes are comfortable in summer and dark ones in winter
Student can identify conduction, convection and radiation when water is heated in a pan
visualIdeas: a pan of water on a flame with arrows labelled conduction, convection and radiation

topics.title: Water Cycle
objectives: Student can describe the water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation into clouds and precipitation
Student can explain how the water cycle redistributes and replenishes water in rivers, lakes and oceans
visualIdeas: a water cycle diagram with the Sun, sea, clouds, rain and plants

topics.title: Seepage of Water Beneath the Earth
objectives: Student can explain why water seeps fastest through gravel and slowest through clay
Student can define infiltration, groundwater and aquifers
Student can explain why groundwater is depleting and how rainwater harvesting and recharge pits help
visualIdeas: three bottles of clay, sand and gravel dripping water into beakers
a cross-section of soil showing an aquifer and a well

topics.title: Measurement of Time
objectives: Student can explain how people used repeating natural events such as day and night, phases of the Moon and seasons to keep time
Student can describe how sundials, water clocks, hourglasses and candle clocks measured time
visualIdeas: a sundial casting a shadow
an hourglass and a floating-bowl water clock

topics.title: A Simple Pendulum
objectives: Student can describe a simple pendulum, its bob, mean position and extreme positions, and one oscillation
Student can define the time period of a pendulum and measure it with a stopwatch
Student can state that the time period of a pendulum of a given length is constant at a place
visualIdeas: a pendulum swinging between extreme positions A and B through mean position O

topics.title: SI Unit of Time
objectives: Student can state that the SI unit of time is the second (s) and convert between seconds, minutes and hours
Student can write units of time and their symbols correctly
visualIdeas: a clock face with 60 s = 1 min and 60 min = 1 h

topics.title: Slow or Fast
objectives: Student can decide who is faster in a race by comparing distances covered in the same time or times taken for the same distance
Student can explain that comparing who is faster needs both the distance covered and the time taken
visualIdeas: runners on a straight track at the same moment

topics.title: Speed
objectives: Student can define speed as the distance covered in unit time and calculate average speed as total distance divided by total time
Student can use the relationship to find distance or time when speed and the other quantity are known
visualIdeas: a speed-distance-time triangle
a car with an odometer and a clock

topics.title: Uniform and Non-uniform Linear Motion
objectives: Student can define linear motion and tell uniform linear motion (constant speed) from non-uniform linear motion (changing speed)
Student can identify uniform or non-uniform motion from a table of distances covered in equal time intervals
visualIdeas: a train between two stations with equally and unequally spaced markers

topics.title: Digestion in Human Beings: Mouth to Stomach
objectives: Student can name the parts of the alimentary canal in order and the associated liver and pancreas
Student can explain mechanical digestion by teeth and how saliva starts digesting starch (chapati tastes sweet on chewing)
Student can describe the role of the stomach and its digestive juice, acid and mucus
visualIdeas: an outline of the human digestive system with labels

topics.title: Digestion in Human Beings: Intestines and Absorption
objectives: Student can explain that digested food is mainly absorbed through the walls of the small intestine and carried by blood
Student can state that the large intestine absorbs most of the remaining water and some salts
visualIdeas: the small intestine with nutrients passing into blood vessels

topics.title: Do All Animals Digest Food the Same Way as Humans Do?
objectives: Student can explain rumination in grass-eating animals such as cows
Student can explain how birds break food in the gizzard with the help of grit
visualIdeas: a cow chewing cud with its rumen marked
a bird digestive system showing the gizzard

topics.title: Respiration in Humans: How Do We Breathe?
objectives: Student can trace the path of air through the nostrils, windpipe and lungs to the alveoli
Student can explain inhalation and exhalation using the movement of the ribs and diaphragm (balloon model)
visualIdeas: a bell-jar balloon model of the lungs and diaphragm
a labelled respiratory system

topics.title: Respiration in Humans: Gas Exchange, Respiration and Circulation
objectives: Student can describe gas exchange between the alveoli and blood
Student can write the word equation of respiration (glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy) and explain that breathing is physical while respiration is chemical
Student can describe the circulatory system: heart, blood and blood vessels transporting nutrients and oxygen
visualIdeas: an alveolus surrounded by a blood vessel with O2 and CO2 arrows
a heart pumping blood through vessels

topics.title: Do Other Animals Breathe the Same Way as Humans Do?
objectives: Student can explain how fish breathe through gills and earthworms through moist skin
Student can explain how frogs use gills as tadpoles and lungs and skin as adults
visualIdeas: a fish with gills highlighted
the life stages of a frog with their breathing organs

topics.title: How Do Plants Grow?
objectives: Student can design and interpret a three-pot experiment testing the role of sunlight and water in plant growth
Student can record changes in height, number and colour of leaves to conclude that sunlight and water are needed for growth
visualIdeas: three potted saplings: in sunlight with water, without water, and in the dark

topics.title: Leaves: the Food Factories of Plants
objectives: Student can explain that leaves contain the green pigment chlorophyll and produce starch
Student can describe the iodine test for starch in a leaf (blue-black colour)
visualIdeas: a decolourised leaf turning blue-black with iodine

topics.title: Role of Air in the Preparation of Food
objectives: Student can describe the experiment with a destarched leaf half inside a bottle of caustic soda
Student can conclude that carbon dioxide from air is needed to make food
visualIdeas: a leaf half inside a bottle with caustic soda, half outside

topics.title: Photosynthesis: In a Nutshell
objectives: Student can write the word equation of photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll
Student can explain that glucose is a source of energy and is stored as starch
visualIdeas: the photosynthesis word equation with a sun and a green leaf

topics.title: How Do Leaves Exchange Gases during Photosynthesis?
objectives: Student can observe stomata in a leaf peel under a microscope
Student can explain the role of stomata in the exchange of carbon dioxide and oxygen
visualIdeas: a magnified leaf peel showing stomata

topics.title: Transport of Water and Minerals
objectives: Student can explain from the red-ink twig experiment how water moves up the stem
Student can state that xylem transports water and minerals from the roots
visualIdeas: a white flower twig in red ink water turning red

topics.title: Transport of Food
objectives: Student can state that phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts of the plant and that food may be stored in seeds and roots
Student can compare the roles of xylem (water and minerals) and phloem (food)
visualIdeas: a plant with phloem arrows from leaves to roots and seeds

topics.title: Do Plants Respire?
objectives: Student can describe the germinating-seeds experiment where lime water turns milky
Student can explain that plants use oxygen and release carbon dioxide during respiration
visualIdeas: a flask of germinating moong seeds connected to a lime water test tube

topics.title: Sources of Light
objectives: Student can classify objects as luminous or non-luminous
Student can explain that the Moon only reflects sunlight
visualIdeas: the Sun, a candle and a bulb next to the Moon and a book

topics.title: Does Light Travel in a Straight Line?
objectives: Student can explain the matchbox activity in which light reaches the screen only when the holes are in a straight line
Student can conclude from the activity that light travels in a straight line
visualIdeas: three matchboxes with holes in a line between a torch and a screen

topics.title: Light through Transparent, Translucent, and Opaque Materials
objectives: Student can classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque by how much light passes through them
Student can predict and then test whether light passes fully, partially or not at all through materials like glass, tracing paper and cardboard
visualIdeas: a torch beam passing through glass, tracing paper and cardboard

topics.title: Shadow Formation
objectives: Student can explain that a shadow forms when an object blocks light
Student can compare shadows of opaque, translucent and transparent objects
visualIdeas: a torch, an object and its shadow on a screen

topics.title: Reflection of Light
objectives: Student can use a mirror or a shiny plate to change the direction of sunlight
Student can define reflection of light
visualIdeas: a mirror redirecting a sunbeam onto a wall

topics.title: Images Formed in a Plane Mirror
objectives: Student can state that the image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object, erect, cannot be obtained on a screen and is laterally inverted
Student can describe lateral inversion using the image of a word such as AMBULANCE in a mirror
visualIdeas: a pen in front of a mirror with its image behind
the word AMBULANCE seen in a mirror

topics.title: Pinhole Camera
objectives: Student can make a pinhole camera and explain why it forms an inverted image
Student can explain that the inverted image is formed because light from the object travels in straight lines through the pinhole
visualIdeas: a candle flame forming an upside-down image through a pinhole

topics.title: Making Some Useful Items
objectives: Student can explain how a periscope uses two plane mirrors to see objects not directly visible
Student can make a kaleidoscope and explain how mirrors create its patterns
visualIdeas: a Z-shaped periscope with two mirrors
a kaleidoscope pattern

topics.title: Rotation of the Earth: Day and Night
objectives: Student can explain that the Earth rotates from West to East on its axis in about 24 hours
Student can use a globe and a torch to explain the day-night cycle
visualIdeas: a globe lit by a torch with the lit half marked day

topics.title: Rotation of the Earth: Apparent Motion of the Sun and Stars
objectives: Student can explain why the Sun, the Moon and the stars appear to move from East to West
Student can explain why the Pole Star appears nearly stationary while other stars appear to move around it
visualIdeas: a merry-go-round rider seeing trees move the other way
star trails around the Pole Star

topics.title: Revolution of the Earth
objectives: Student can define revolution and orbit
Student can state that the Earth completes one revolution around the Sun in about 365 days and 6 hours
visualIdeas: a top view of the Earth's nearly circular orbit around the Sun

topics.title: Changing View of Night Sky from the Earth
objectives: Student can explain why different stars are seen at sunset in different months
Student can explain that this change is caused by the Earth's revolution around the Sun
visualIdeas: the Earth at four points of its orbit with different stars rising at sunset

topics.title: Seasons on the Earth
objectives: Student can explain that seasons occur because of the tilt of the Earth's axis and its spherical shape
Student can explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer in June and winter in December, and the Southern Hemisphere the reverse
Student can name the solstices and equinoxes
visualIdeas: the tilted Earth in June and December positions around the Sun
sunrays spread over a small and a large area

topics.title: Solar Eclipse
objectives: Student can explain that a solar eclipse occurs when the Moon blocks sunlight from reaching the Earth
Student can explain apparent size using the thumb activity
Student can explain why one must not look directly at the Sun even during a solar eclipse
visualIdeas: Sun, Moon and Earth in a line with the Moon's shadow on the Earth

topics.title: Lunar Eclipse
objectives: Student can explain that a lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
Student can tell a total lunar eclipse from a partial one
visualIdeas: the Moon passing through the Earth's shadow, turning dark red
